name: Grace Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Grace, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you're free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a timber-frame company, and right now we're putting up houses on a new estate on the edge of town, sixty-odd homes in a field that had sheep on it last year. The wall panels come from a factory two hours away, and we stand them up, fix them, put the roof cassettes on, and then do the general carpentry inside. I'm on site at seven, and before anything I take photos of the drawings and ask the AI on my phone to give me the cut list and spot anything that doesn't match. It catches mistakes maybe once a week, which saves us a whole morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the day a house goes from a slab to a shape, you can almost see the family in it. What grinds me down is the pay, which is low for the trade because there's really only us and one other firm round here. Marcus drives buses and we've got Hana and Leo, so with the mortgage there's nothing left at the end of the month, I mean actually nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but it's still useful, and I'd show people how I use it on my phone. I'm the one on site who sends the AI tips to the group chat. I'd probably post something like 'not the robot uprising, just a very good assistant'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the tools and I'd hoped they'd make the job less brutal on the body. But for the bank account it changes nothing, which is the actual problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, using it for cut lists and checks, maybe for writing up the snag lists faster. I'd push the union branch to talk about pay, because that's the real issue whether AI happens or not. I might use it to price up a few weekend jobs, decking or sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Nothing breaks, but nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hoped it would make the job less brutal. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shoulders are forty-three going on sixty. I'd hoped for a machine that lifts the panels while I guide them, not a phone that writes my emails. In this picture we get the phone but not the arms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do people on site ever push back when you share AI tips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older lads roll their eyes, Pete calls it my 'little oracle'. But he asked me to check his kid's maths homework with it last week. So the eye-rolling has limits.

S0.say: It was oversold but still useful, and she'd show people how she uses it on site. She'd post something like 'not the robot uprising, just a very good assistant'.
S0.think: She'd be a little disappointed, having hoped the tools would make the job easier on her body. Financially it changes nothing, which is the real problem.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for cut lists, checks and snag lists, and pushes the union branch on pay. Uses it to price a few weekend decking or shed jobs.
S0.feel: Calm but a bit flat: nothing breaks, nothing improves.
S0.quote: In this picture we get the phone but not the arms.
S0.fieldNote: Grace is an enthusiastic everyday AI user who wanted more from it, especially physical help. Her real grievance is pay, not technology. She's the informal tech guide on her crew, even for sceptics like Pete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to make the job better if workers are in the room when the decisions get made. Robots on site could save a lot of backs and knees. But the union needs to make sure the gains get shared and nobody's thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm better placed than most. We already build from factory panels, so the jump to more automation isn't as big for us. If I'm the person who can run the new kit, I'm the last one they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company straight away to put me on any training for new machinery, the panel cranes, layout robots, whatever. I'd do online courses at night, the free ones, while Marcus does the kids' bedtime. And I'd push the union to get a deal that says operators get paid more, not the same for more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe even a bit excited. Worried for some of the others, but for me it looks like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're worried for the others. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, mostly. He's fifty-five and brilliant with his hands, but he doesn't want to touch a tablet. If the job becomes 'watch the screen', he's the one I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With savings as thin as you've described, isn't taking on courses at night risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's risky not to. The free courses cost me sleep, not money. And if it ends up with an extra couple of pounds an hour as an operator, that's the first time in years the maths would go our way.

S1.say: It's a chance to make the job better if workers are in the room: robots could save backs and knees, but the union must ensure gains are shared and nobody is thrown out.
S1.think: She thinks she's better placed than most because her firm already builds from factory panels. If she's the one who can run the new kit, she'll be the last let go.
S1.do: Asks the company to put her on training for any new machinery and takes free online courses at night. Pushes the union for a deal that pays operators more.
S1.feel: Calm and even a little excited, though worried for older colleagues.
S1.quote: The free courses cost me sleep, not money.
S1.fieldNote: This is where Grace's adaptability shows most: she sees a door opening and walks towards it. She also has a clear sense of fairness, wanting operators paid more and colleagues like Pete protected. Thin savings push her towards free training rather than holding her back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest shift in working life ever, and leaving it to a handful of tech companies would be madness. Public ownership of some of it, a proper income floor, and workers sharing in what the robots earn. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being quick with tech won't save me in two years. If AI plus robots can do the whole job, my being good with the phone just means I'm the last person to be told, not that I'm kept. And we have nothing in the bank to ride out even three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month, I'd sit down with Marcus and cut everything that isn't food, mortgage or heating. I'd try to get hired as one of the people who sets up and maintains the robots on site, even on a short contract, because someone has to do it at first. I'd also get a group of us together to see if we could form a small co-op, rent a robot ourselves and take the small jobs the big firms won't bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed, not the change. I can learn fast, but not that fast, and not with an empty account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the co-op idea. Who would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, Pete if he'd come, Aisha from the joinery firm, maybe two others. We'd pool what little we have, lease one machine, and do extensions and repairs for local people. It's not a fortune, but it's ours, and the profit doesn't go off to some head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you do in the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn everything I could about the robots, how they're set up, what goes wrong, how you fix them. And I'd stop spending on anything that isn't necessary, start a tiny emergency pot. Two years is enough to get a head start, not enough to get safe.

S2.say: This is the biggest shift in working life ever and can't be left to a few tech companies: she wants partial public ownership, an income floor and workers sharing in what robots earn. She'd be organising, not just posting.
S2.think: Being quick with tech won't save her in two years; it just means she's the last told. With nothing in the bank, the family couldn't ride out even three months.
S2.do: Cuts everything except food, mortgage and heating, and tries for a short contract setting up and maintaining site robots. Gathers colleagues to form a small co-op that leases a robot for local repair and extension work.
S2.feel: Alarmed by the speed: she can learn fast, but not that fast with an empty account.
S2.quote: It's the speed, not the change.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability doesn't shield her from the money problem, and she says so plainly. Her instinct is collective and practical: a co-op with named colleagues rather than going it alone. She's both organising politically and grabbing any role near the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it, but only if we start now. I'd want robot companies to have to train local workers to maintain their machines, as a condition of selling them here. And I'd be loud about it at the union and with the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years could work for me. If I spend two of them becoming the person who can install, check and repair the robots on timber-frame sites, I'm worth something when they arrive. I'd be forty-eight with a skill that's in demand for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start right away on a part-time course in robotics maintenance or building automation, evenings and weekends, paid for by the union or a grant. I'd keep the job while I learn, so the mortgage doesn't slip. By the time it lands, I'd want a certificate and a foot in the door with the company that sells the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited underneath. There's a lot to do, and I like having a lot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm scrambling for crumbs. With five, I get to train properly and walk in the door with something they need. That's a whole different conversation with the bank manager too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but later, and smarter. With five years, we could save up, plan it, maybe get a council start-up grant. Doing it in a panic is how you lose your house.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ahead of it only if action starts now: robot companies should have to train local workers to maintain their machines. She'd push this at the union and the council.
S3.think: Five years could work for her: by spending two becoming a robot installer and repairer for timber-frame sites, she'd be valuable on arrival at forty-eight.
S3.do: Starts a part-time robotics maintenance or building automation course straight away, funded by the union or a grant, while keeping her job. Aims for a certificate and a foot in the door with the robot supplier, and plans the co-op later with savings and a start-up grant.
S3.feel: Anxious but excited underneath, glad to have a lot to do.
S3.quote: Doing it in a panic is how you lose your house.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Grace's scramble into a plan, and she's precise about how she'd use the time. She keeps the job while she trains, which reflects her thin savings. She still wants public rules, like making robot companies train local workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do it right: proper public training, workers on company boards, and a share of the gains for everyone. No excuses with that much warning. I'd say it at the union, online, and to every politician who knocks on my door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like an opportunity more than a threat. I'd have time to train, build up the co-op slowly, maybe even get Marcus involved on the van side. Hana and Leo would be teenagers, and I'd want them to see their mum do it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start the robotics course and keep working. I'd talk to the union about a pilot co-op with a couple of others, saving a little each month towards it. I'd sit down with the kids and talk about what they want to learn, and I'd spend my evenings learning, not scrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried. Ten years is time to make something good out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still scares you, even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people at the top make all the decisions in the first two years while we're busy paying bills. Ten years is plenty of time for us, but it's also plenty of time for them to lock it all up. That's why I'd stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the world's going to need people who understand machines and people who understand people. Hana's the people one, Leo's the machine one. And I'd tell them both, don't let anyone tell you that you don't get a say.

S4.say: A decade is time to do it right: public training, workers on company boards and a share of the gains for everyone. She'd say so at the union, online and to every politician at her door.
S4.think: Ten years feels more like an opportunity than a threat: time to train, build the co-op slowly, maybe involve Marcus, and show her children it can be done well.
S4.do: Starts the robotics course while still working and proposes a pilot co-op through the union, saving a little each month towards it. Talks with her children about what they want to learn and spends evenings studying.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than worried.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty of time for us, but it's also plenty of time for them to lock it all up.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Grace's hope comes forward, but her fear shifts from her own job to who controls the change. She keeps coming back to collective ownership and workers' voice. She thinks about her children as part of the plan, not just as dependants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to do anything properly and we have no savings to buy time. What would help is a guaranteed income for a year or two while people retrain, and rules that say the robot makers have to train local workers to look after their machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my body. Everyone imagines a robot taking our jobs, but the honest truth is half of us on site are in pain most days. If we got the arms and kept the pay, I'd take that version in a heartbeat.

headlineQuote: If we got the arms and kept the pay, I'd take that version in a heartbeat.
portrait: Grace Tanaka is a 43-year-old timber-frame carpenter on a new housing estate, a daily AI user who checks drawings with her phone, but with nothing left at the end of each month. In AI Plateau she's a little disappointed; in Steady Disruption she sees a door opening and heads for machinery training. AGI by 2028 alarms her because her speed with technology can't beat the empty bank account, so she turns to a co-op and any work near the robots. With five or ten years she plans a proper route into robot maintenance and a slow-built co-op. She believes workers should share in what the robots earn and fears the decisions being locked up at the top.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to do anything properly and no savings to buy time.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a year or two while people retrain, and rules making robot makers train local workers to look after their machines.
